data.answer:
For **Australians seeking protection overseas**, the evidence shows substantial use of PCT and Madrid, but does not quantify Hague use.

- **Patents — PCT:** The **2017 report** recorded that Australians used the PCT for **67 per cent of 8,562 overseas patent applications**, with 33 per cent filed directly. It described this split as similar to the preceding 10 years.[1]
- **Trade marks — Madrid:** The **2026 report** provides more recent outbound figures: **56.6 per cent of Australian trade mark classes filed abroad in 2024** went through Madrid, up from 45.0 per cent in 2019. These are class counts, not application counts.[2]
- **Designs — Hague:** No Australian usage share or volume is provided. The Hague system allows applicants to seek design registration in multiple countries through one international application. The **2024 report** said Australia had agreed to make all reasonable efforts to join under the Australia–UK free trade agreement; it did not report completed accession.[3]

The PCT and Madrid percentages are therefore **not directly comparable**: they refer to different periods and counting units.[1][2]

citations.quote: Of the 8562 applications filed by Australians overseas, 33 per cent were directly filed with overseas patent offices while 67 per cent used the PCT route
This level of usage of the PCT route is similar to that observed over the last 10 years.

claims.text: The 2017 report recorded PCT use for 67 per cent of Australians’ 8,562 overseas patent applications, versus 33 per cent direct, consistent with the preceding decade.

citations.quote: the share of Australian classes filed abroad through the Madrid system has increased, from 45.0% in 2019 to 56.6% in 2024.

claims.text: The 2026 report states that Madrid accounted for 56.6 per cent of Australian trade mark classes filed abroad in 2024, up from 45.0 per cent in 2019; this measures classes rather than applications.

citations.quote: The Hague Agreement on Industrial Designs allows design applicants to seek registration in multiple countries through a single international application.
In principle, Australia has agreed to make all reasonable efforts to join the Hague Agreement as part of a free trade agreement (FTA) between Australia and the UK.

claims.text: Hague provides a single international design application route; the 2024 report described Australia’s commitment to make reasonable efforts to join, rather than completed accession.

gaps: No recent outbound PCT usage figures for Australians are supplied; the latest supplied outbound percentage is in the 2017 report.
No volume or share of Australians’ Hague filings is supplied, nor confirmation of Australia’s accession after the 2024 report.
The passages do not provide a same-year comparison across all three systems using a common counting unit.
